questions.q: Why can a company report strong net income while actually running low on cash?
options: This situation is impossible under any accounting method
Because net income always equals cash flow by definition
Because the company must be committing fraud
Because net income is an accrual-basis number, and revenue earned doesn't always mean cash has been collected yet
questions.explain: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recognized when earned, which can outpace actual cash collections — growing receivables is a common example.

questions.q: Which of the three cash flow statement categories includes buying new equipment?
options: Operating activities
Investing activities
Financing activities
None of the three categories cover equipment purchases
questions.explain: Investing activities cover cash spent on or received from long-term assets, such as purchasing equipment.

questions.q: Which category includes proceeds from a new loan?
options: Operating activities
Investing activities
Financing activities
This would not appear anywhere on a cash flow statement
questions.explain: Financing activities cover cash from or paid to owners and lenders, including loan proceeds and repayments.

questions.q: In the Pemberton Craft Supply example, net income was $92,000 but the net increase in cash was $50,000. What explains most of the difference?
options: A $30,000 increase in Accounts Receivable (cash not yet collected) and a $50,000 equipment purchase, partly offset by a $20,000 new loan and adding back $18,000 of depreciation
The company simply made a bookkeeping error
Net income and cash flow are always identical, so this scenario is impossible
The difference is entirely due to foreign currency translation
questions.explain: The operating, investing, and financing adjustments together reconcile accrual-based net income to the actual $50,000 increase in cash.

questions.q: Why do lenders pay such close attention to the cash flow statement?
options: Because lenders only care about a company's logo and branding
Because the cash flow statement is required to be shorter than the other two statements
Lenders typically ignore the cash flow statement entirely
Because they care whether the company generates enough actual operating cash to make loan payments, not just whether it looks profitable on an accrual basis
questions.explain: Lenders are focused on real cash availability for debt service, which is exactly what the cash flow statement is designed to reveal.
